title: Support and Transport Systems in Plants
seo_title: Grade 10 Life Sciences: Support and Transport Systems in Plants Worksheets (CAPS)
standard_code: Grade 10 Life Sciences: Support and transport systems in plants
standard_text: The structure of roots, stems and leaves; the transport of water and minerals in the xylem (absorption by roots, root pressure, capillarity and transpiration pull); transpiration and the factors that affect it; translocation of food in the phloem. (summary of CAPS Life Sciences, Grade 10, Life Sciences: Support and transport systems in plants)
meta_desc: Free Grade 10 Life Sciences worksheets (CAPS): roots, stems and leaves, xylem and phloem, transpiration and its factors, and translocation. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Transpiration pulls water up the xylem.
key_sub: Phloem moves sugars from leaves to other parts.
body_html:
How to think about it

Root hairs absorb water by osmosis and minerals by active transport. Water moves up the xylem by root pressure, capillarity and mainly the transpiration pull: water evaporates from the leaves through the stomata, pulling a column of water up the stem.

Transpiration is faster when it is hot, dry, windy and bright. Guard cells open and close the stomata. Translocation carries sugars made in the leaves through the phloem to growing parts and storage organs.

Example

Why does a plant wilt on a hot, windy day?

It loses water faster than it takes it in.

Answer: transpiration is faster than water uptake

Example

What do guard cells control?

They surround a pore.

Answer: the opening and closing of stomata

Common mistakes

  • Thinking water is pumped up by the heart of the plant.
  • Thinking transpiration happens through the roots.
  • Mixing up xylem and phloem.

faq.a: They are long and thin with a large surface area for absorbing water and minerals.

faq.q: Why do plants close their stomata at night?
faq.a: There is no light for photosynthesis, so closing them saves water.

items.q: Which feature is typical of a sperm cell?
c: no cytoplasm or cross-walls and lignified walls
items.e: A sperm cell has a tail (flagellum) and many mitochondria: energy to swim to the egg.

items.q: Which cell has a long, narrow extension, giving a larger surface area to absorb water and mineral salts?
c: a pancreatic cell that secretes enzymes
items.e: Each specialised cell is adapted to its job.

items.q: Which tissue or structure is described as dead cells with thick lignified walls that give mechanical support?
items.e: Sclerenchyma: dead cells with thick lignified walls that give mechanical support.

items.q: A sperm cell has a tail (flagellum) and many mitochondria. How does this help it?
c: a change of shape that opens and closes the stoma
a larger surface area to absorb water and mineral salts
an empty, continuous tube that carries water and gives support
energy to swim to the egg
items.e: Structure fits function.

items.q: Which description fits phloem?
c: large empty cells in grass leaves that make them roll up in dry weather
openings in the bark for gas exchange
cells that open and close the stomatal pore
items.e: Phloem: transporting food from leaves.

items.q: Which cells guard the stomata of grasses?
items.e: Dicots have bean-shaped guard cells.

items.q: Which description fits parenchyma?
c: a waxy layer on the epidermis that cuts water loss
dead cells with thick lignified walls that give mechanical support
thin-walled living cells used for storage and photosynthesis
parenchyma cells between the vascular bundles of a dicot stem
items.e: Parenchyma: thin-walled living cells used for storage and photosynthesis.

items.q: What is the outermost layer of the primary plant body?
items.e: It is covered by cuticle in shoots.

items.q: What is a dorsiventral leaf?
c: a leaf with palisade on the upper side and spongy tissue below, as in dicots
a leaf with the same tissue on both sides
items.e: Isobilateral leaves (grasses) differ.

items.q: Which feature is typical of a pancreatic cell that secretes enzymes?
c: a lot of rough endoplasmic reticulum and a large Golgi body
items.e: A pancreatic cell that secretes enzymes has a lot of rough endoplasmic reticulum and a large Golgi body: many proteins made and packaged for secretion.

items.q: Which description fits spongy parenchyma?
c: loosely arranged cells with air spaces in the lower part of a dicot leaf
the layers just below the epidermis, of collenchyma in dicot stems
thin-walled living cells used for storage and photosynthesis
cells that open and close the stomatal pore
items.e: Spongy parenchyma: loosely arranged cells with air spaces in the lower part of a dicot leaf.

items.q: A guard cell has a thicker inner wall. How does this help it?
c: a change of shape that opens and closes the stoma
a larger surface area to absorb water and mineral salts
an empty, continuous tube that carries water and gives support
many proteins made and packaged for secretion
items.e: Structure fits function.

items.q: Which plants have no secondary growth usually?
items.e: They lack a vascular cambium.

items.q: Which feature is typical of a xylem vessel?
c: no cytoplasm or cross-walls and lignified walls
items.e: A xylem vessel has no cytoplasm or cross-walls and lignified walls: an empty, continuous tube that carries water and gives support.

items.q: Which feature is typical of a red blood cell?
c: no cytoplasm or cross-walls and lignified walls
no nucleus and a biconcave shape
items.e: A red blood cell has no nucleus and a biconcave shape: more room for haemoglobin and a larger surface area to take up oxygen.

items.q: A xylem vessel has no cytoplasm or cross-walls and lignified walls. How does this help it?
c: more room for haemoglobin and a larger surface area to take up oxygen
an empty, continuous tube that carries water and gives support
energy to swim to the egg
many proteins made and packaged for secretion
items.e: Structure fits function.

items.q: Which description fits guard cells?
c: cells that open and close the stomatal pore
specialised parenchyma cells linked to sieve tubes
cork, the dead outer layer of bark
dead cells with thick lignified walls that give mechanical support
items.e: Guard cells: cells that open and close the stomatal pore.

items.q: A red blood cell has no nucleus and a biconcave shape. How does this help it?
c: many proteins made and packaged for secretion
more room for haemoglobin and a larger surface area to take up oxygen
energy to swim to the egg
more energy released by respiration for contraction
items.e: Structure fits function.

items.q: Which cell has many chloroplasts, giving more light absorbed for photosynthesis?
c: a pancreatic cell that secretes enzymes
items.e: Each specialised cell is adapted to its job.

items.q: Which tissue or structure is described as the layer just inside the endodermis that gives rise to lateral roots?
items.e: Pericycle: the layer just inside the endodermis that gives rise to lateral roots.

items.q: Which plant has a fibrous root system?
items.e: Monocots like wheat have fibrous roots.

items.q: What is a racemose inflorescence?
c: one in which the main axis keeps growing and flowers form laterally
items.e: Flowers open from the base upward.

items.q: Which phyllotaxy does Alstonia have?
items.e: More than two leaves at each node.

items.q: In which organ is this seen: radial vascular bundles, 2–4 xylem bundles and a small pith?
items.e: Dicot root: radial vascular bundles, 2–4 xylem bundles and a small pith.

items.q: What is phyllotaxy?
c: the pattern in which leaves are arranged on a stem
items.e: Alternate, opposite or whorled.

items.q: Which description fits a dicot root?
c: radial vascular bundles, more than six xylem bundles and a large pith
scattered vascular bundles, conjoint and closed, with a bundle sheath
vascular bundles in a ring, conjoint, open, with cambium
radial vascular bundles, 2–4 xylem bundles and a small pith
items.e: Dicot root: radial vascular bundles, 2–4 xylem bundles and a small pith.

items.q: What are stamens attached to petals called?
items.e: e.g. brinjal.

items.q: Which description fits collenchyma?
c: cells that open and close the stomatal pore
a waxy layer on the epidermis that cuts water loss
living cells thickened at the corners with cellulose and pectin
loosely arranged cells with air spaces in the lower part of a dicot leaf
items.e: Collenchyma: living cells thickened at the corners with cellulose and pectin.

items.q: From which tissue do lateral roots arise?
items.e: It also helps form vascular cambium in roots.

items.q: Which description fits a monocot stem?
c: radial vascular bundles, 2–4 xylem bundles and a small pith
vascular bundles in a ring, conjoint, open, with cambium
scattered vascular bundles, conjoint and closed, with a bundle sheath
radial vascular bundles, more than six xylem bundles and a large pith
items.e: Monocot stem: scattered vascular bundles, conjoint and closed, with a bundle sheath.

items.q: What does the vascular cambium produce?
c: secondary xylem on the inside and secondary phloem on the outside
items.e: This causes growth in girth.

items.q: Which part of phloem is absent in gymnosperms?
items.e: They have albuminous cells and sieve cells.

items.q: Which description fits hypodermis?
c: a waxy layer on the epidermis that cuts water loss
the layers just below the epidermis, of collenchyma in dicot stems
tall, closely packed cells with many chloroplasts below the upper epidermis
the cork cambium that makes cork and secondary cortex
items.e: Hypodermis: the layers just below the epidermis, of collenchyma in dicot stems.

items.q: Which description fits a monocot root?
c: radial vascular bundles, 2–4 xylem bundles and a small pith
radial vascular bundles, more than six xylem bundles and a large pith
vascular bundles in a ring, conjoint, open, with cambium
scattered vascular bundles, conjoint and closed, with a bundle sheath
items.e: Monocot root: radial vascular bundles, more than six xylem bundles and a large pith.

items.q: Which description fits a dicot stem?
c: vascular bundles in a ring, conjoint, open, with cambium
radial vascular bundles, 2–4 xylem bundles and a small pith
scattered vascular bundles, conjoint and closed, with a bundle sheath
radial vascular bundles, more than six xylem bundles and a large pith
items.e: Dicot stem: vascular bundles in a ring, conjoint, open, with cambium.

items.q: Which root system do dicots usually have?
items.e: The primary root goes on growing.

items.q: In which organ is this seen: radial vascular bundles, more than six xylem bundles and a large pith?
items.e: Monocot root: radial vascular bundles, more than six xylem bundles and a large pith.

items.q: Which elements of xylem are found mainly in angiosperms?
items.e: Gymnosperms lack vessels.

items.q: Which description fits lenticels?
c: living cells thickened at the corners with cellulose and pectin
cells that open and close the stomatal pore
openings in the bark for gas exchange
items.e: Lenticels: openings in the bark for gas exchange.

items.q: Which tissue or structure is described as conducting water and minerals from roots?
items.e: Xylem: conducting water and minerals from roots.

items.q: In a potometer, the air bubble moves 4 cm along the tube in 2 minutes. What is the rate of water uptake in cm per minute?
items.e: Rate = distance ÷ time = 4 ÷ 2.

items.q: What is the effect of brighter light on the rate of transpiration?
items.e: Transpiration is faster when the air is warm, dry and moving and the stomata are open in light.

items.q: In 10 minutes an air bubble in a potometer moves 40 mm along a capillary tube of radius 0,50 mm. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹.
items.e: Volume = πr²d = π × 0,50² × 40 = 31,4 mm³; ÷ 10 min = 3,14 mm³ min⁻¹.

items.q: In a potometer, the air bubble moves 6 cm along the tube in 4 minutes. What is the rate of water uptake in cm per minute?
items.e: Rate = distance ÷ time = 6 ÷ 4.

items.q: What is the effect of darkness (stomata close) on the rate of transpiration?
items.e: Transpiration is faster when the air is warm, dry and moving and the stomata are open in light.

items.q: What is root pressure?
c: active loading of ions into the xylem in roots lowers water potential so water enters
items.e: It only pushes water a short distance.

items.q: What is the effect of drier air on the rate of transpiration?
items.e: Transpiration is faster when the air is warm, dry and moving and the stomata are open in light.

items.q: In 10 minutes an air bubble in a potometer moves 50 mm along a capillary tube of radius 1,0 mm. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹.
items.e: Volume = πr²d = π × 1,0² × 50 = 157 mm³; ÷ 10 min = 15,7 mm³ min⁻¹.

items.q: What does a ringing experiment show?
c: removing the phloem makes sugars build up above the ring
items.e: Evidence that phloem carries organic substances.

items.q: In 10 minutes an air bubble in a potometer moves 50 mm along a capillary tube of radius 0,40 mm. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹.
items.e: Volume = πr²d = π × 0,40² × 50 = 25,1 mm³; ÷ 10 min = 2,51 mm³ min⁻¹.

items.q: What is a source in translocation?
c: where sugars are made or released, such as a leaf
where sugars are used or stored
items.e: A sink uses or stores sugars.

items.q: What is the effect of higher temperature on the rate of transpiration?
items.e: Transpiration is faster when the air is warm, dry and moving and the stomata are open in light.

items.q: What is the effect of lower temperature on the rate of transpiration?
items.e: Transpiration is faster when the air is warm, dry and moving and the stomata are open in light.

items.q: In 2 minutes an air bubble in a potometer moves 50 mm along a capillary tube of radius 1,0 mm. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹.
items.e: Volume = πr²d = π × 1,0² × 50 = 157 mm³; ÷ 2 min = 78,5 mm³ min⁻¹.

items.q: In a potometer, the air bubble moves 8 cm along the tube in 10 minutes. What is the rate of water uptake in cm per minute?
items.e: Rate = distance ÷ time = 8 ÷ 10.

items.q: What does a potometer actually measure?
c: water uptake, which is close to the rate of transpiration
items.e: Some water is used in photosynthesis.

items.q: What is the mass flow hypothesis?
c: sucrose loaded at the source lowers water potential, water enters and pressure pushes the sap to the sink
items.e: Sinks include roots and growing tips.

items.q: In 2 minutes an air bubble in a potometer moves 30 mm along a capillary tube of radius 0,40 mm. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹.
items.e: Volume = πr²d = π × 0,40² × 30 = 15,1 mm³; ÷ 2 min = 7,54 mm³ min⁻¹.

items.q: In 10 minutes an air bubble in a potometer moves 25 mm along a capillary tube of radius 1,0 mm. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹.
items.e: Volume = πr²d = π × 1,0² × 25 = 78,5 mm³; ÷ 10 min = 7,85 mm³ min⁻¹.

items.q: In a potometer, the air bubble moves 5 cm along the tube in 4 minutes. What is the rate of water uptake in cm per minute?
items.e: Rate = distance ÷ time = 5 ÷ 4.

items.q: In 5 minutes an air bubble in a potometer moves 50 mm along a capillary tube of radius 0,40 mm. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹.
items.e: Volume = πr²d = π × 0,40² × 50 = 25,1 mm³; ÷ 5 min = 5,03 mm³ min⁻¹.

items.q: Which digestive enzyme breaks down starch?
items.e: Amylase is made in the salivary glands and pancreas.

items.q: How do radioactive tracers show translocation?
c: ¹⁴CO₂ is supplied to a leaf and labelled sugars are found in the phloem
dye shows water in the xylem
items.e: Autoradiography shows the path.

items.q: What is the correct order of organisation in a multicellular organism?
items.e: Specialised cells form tissues.

items.q: In 2 minutes an air bubble in a potometer moves 45 mm along a capillary tube of radius 1,0 mm. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹.
items.e: Volume = πr²d = π × 1,0² × 45 = 141 mm³; ÷ 2 min = 70,7 mm³ min⁻¹.

items.q: In 6 minutes an air bubble in a potometer moves 15 mm along a capillary tube of radius 0,25 mm. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹.
items.e: Volume = πr²d = π × 0,25² × 15 = 2,95 mm³; ÷ 6 min = 0,491 mm³ min⁻¹.

items.q: In 6 minutes an air bubble in a potometer moves 25 mm along a capillary tube of radius 1,0 mm. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹.
items.e: Volume = πr²d = π × 1,0² × 25 = 78,5 mm³; ÷ 6 min = 13,1 mm³ min⁻¹.

items.q: What is the cohesion–tension theory?
c: root pressure pushes all water up
water evaporating from leaves pulls a continuous column of water up the xylem
items.e: Hydrogen bonds hold the water molecules together.

items.q: In 6 minutes an air bubble in a potometer moves 20 mm along a capillary tube of radius 0,75 mm. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹.
items.e: Volume = πr²d = π × 0,75² × 20 = 35,3 mm³; ÷ 6 min = 5,89 mm³ min⁻¹.

items.q: What are companion cells for?
c: providing ATP for active loading of sucrose into sieve tubes
items.e: They have many mitochondria.

items.q: Why is lignin present in xylem walls?
c: it strengthens the vessels so they do not collapse
items.e: Xylem vessels are dead with no end walls.

items.q: Why do stomata close at night in most plants?
c: there is no light for photosynthesis, so closing reduces water loss
items.e: Guard cells lose turgor.

items.q: In 5 minutes an air bubble in a potometer moves 12 mm along a capillary tube of radius 0,40 mm. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹.
items.e: Volume = πr²d = π × 0,40² × 12 = 6,03 mm³; ÷ 5 min = 1,21 mm³ min⁻¹.

items.q: What is transpiration?
c: the loss of water vapour from the leaves through the stomata
items.e: It pulls water up the xylem.

items.q: In 10 minutes an air bubble in a potometer moves 20 mm along a capillary tube of radius 0,25 mm. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹.
items.e: Volume = πr²d = π × 0,25² × 20 = 3,93 mm³; ÷ 10 min = 0,393 mm³ min⁻¹.

items.q: Which blood vessels carry blood away from the heart at high pressure?
items.e: Arteries have thick, elastic walls.

items.q: Why must a potometer be set up under water?
c: to stop air entering the xylem and the apparatus
items.e: An airlock would stop the water column.

items.q: What does phloem transport?
items.e: This is translocation.

items.q: In 2 minutes an air bubble in a potometer moves 50 mm along a capillary tube of radius 0,25 mm. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹.
items.e: Volume = πr²d = π × 0,25² × 50 = 9,82 mm³; ÷ 2 min = 4,91 mm³ min⁻¹.

items.q: What is cell differentiation?
c: a cell losing all its DNA
a cell becoming specialised for one function by switching on particular genes
items.e: All body cells have the same genes but use different ones.

sets.title: Anatomy of roots, stems and leaves

items.q: Which tissue or structure is described as cells that open and close the stomatal pore?
items.e: Guard cells: cells that open and close the stomatal pore.

items.q: Which tissue or structure is described as thin-walled living cells used for storage and photosynthesis?
items.e: Parenchyma: thin-walled living cells used for storage and photosynthesis.

items.q: In which organ is this seen: scattered vascular bundles, conjoint and closed, with a bundle sheath?
items.e: Monocot stem: scattered vascular bundles, conjoint and closed, with a bundle sheath.

items.q: What are annual rings?
c: the rings of the bark only
rings of spring wood and autumn wood formed each year
items.e: They are used to estimate a tree's age.

items.q: Which description fits medullary rays?
c: loosely arranged cells with air spaces in the lower part of a dicot leaf
thin-walled living cells used for storage and photosynthesis
parenchyma cells between the vascular bundles of a dicot stem
the innermost layer of the cortex, with Casparian strips in roots
items.e: Medullary rays: parenchyma cells between the vascular bundles of a dicot stem.

items.q: What is the periderm made of?
items.e: It replaces the epidermis in older stems.

items.q: Which tissue or structure is described as parenchyma cells between the vascular bundles of a dicot stem?
items.e: Medullary rays: parenchyma cells between the vascular bundles of a dicot stem.

items.q: Which description fits palisade parenchyma?
c: tall, closely packed cells with many chloroplasts below the upper epidermis
parenchyma cells between the vascular bundles of a dicot stem
the layer just inside the endodermis that gives rise to lateral roots
openings in the bark for gas exchange
items.e: Palisade parenchyma: tall, closely packed cells with many chloroplasts below the upper epidermis.

items.q: What is endarch xylem?
c: protoxylem towards the centre and metaxylem towards the outside
items.e: Found in stems; roots are exarch.

items.q: What is heartwood?
c: the dark central wood made of dead xylem filled with tannins and resins
items.e: It is durable and no longer conducts water.

items.q: Which description fits xylem?
c: living cells thickened at the corners with cellulose and pectin
the cork cambium that makes cork and secondary cortex
large empty cells in grass leaves that make them roll up in dry weather
conducting water and minerals from roots
items.e: Xylem: conducting water and minerals from roots.

items.q: Which tissue or structure is described as loosely arranged cells with air spaces in the lower part of a dicot leaf?
items.e: Spongy parenchyma: loosely arranged cells with air spaces in the lower part of a dicot leaf.

items.q: Which layer in the root has Casparian strips?
items.e: Suberin blocks water from moving through the walls.

items.q: Which tissue or structure is described as tall, closely packed cells with many chloroplasts below the upper epidermis?
items.e: Palisade parenchyma: tall, closely packed cells with many chloroplasts below the upper epidermis.

items.q: Which description fits sclerenchyma?
c: the layers just below the epidermis, of collenchyma in dicot stems
loosely arranged cells with air spaces in the lower part of a dicot leaf
cells that open and close the stomatal pore
dead cells with thick lignified walls that give mechanical support
items.e: Sclerenchyma: dead cells with thick lignified walls that give mechanical support.

items.q: Which description fits phellogen?
c: the cork cambium that makes cork and secondary cortex
specialised parenchyma cells linked to sieve tubes
dead cells with thick lignified walls that give mechanical support
living cells thickened at the corners with cellulose and pectin
items.e: Phellogen: the cork cambium that makes cork and secondary cortex.

items.q: Which tissue or structure is described as transporting food from leaves?
items.e: Phloem: transporting food from leaves.

items.q: Which tissue or structure is described as the layers just below the epidermis, of collenchyma in dicot stems?
items.e: Hypodermis: the layers just below the epidermis, of collenchyma in dicot stems.

items.q: In which organ is this seen: vascular bundles in a ring, conjoint, open, with cambium?
items.e: Dicot stem: vascular bundles in a ring, conjoint, open, with cambium.

items.q: Which tissue or structure is described as living cells thickened at the corners with cellulose and pectin?
items.e: Collenchyma: living cells thickened at the corners with cellulose and pectin.
